ABSTRACT
Multimodal recommender systems (MRS) integrate heterogeneous
user and item data, such as text, images, and structured information,
to enhance recommendation performance. The emergence of large
language models (LLMs) introduces new opportunities for MRS
by enabling semantic reasoning, in-context learning, and dynamic
input handling. Compared to earlier pre-trained language models
(PLMs), LLMs offer greater flexibility and generalisation capabilities
but also introduce challenges related to scalability and model ac-
cessibility. This survey presents a comprehensive review of recent
work at the intersection of LLMs and MRS, focusing on prompting
strategies, fine-tuning methods, and data adaptation techniques.
We propose a novel taxonomy to characterise integration patterns,
identify transferable techniques from related recommendation do-

point to possible future directions. We aim to clarify the emerging

Other methods increase complexity or modularity in prompt-
ing. For example, Xi et al . [129] introduce factorisation prompt-
ing, which decomposes recommendation reasoning into smaller
subtasks—each encoded via a separate sub-prompt. This modular
approach improves interpretability and enables better task general-
isation.
A third group of works focuses on deriving prompts directly from
user behaviours or historical data. Lyu et al. [79] utilizes summari-
sation, paraphrasing, recommendation-driven, and engagement-
guided prompts to enhance item description generation; Yin et al.
[139] encodes heterogeneous, multi-type user behaviour logs into
unified text templates; and Paischer et al. [87] designs per-timestep
prompts based on sequential interaction histories and reviews.
Beyond individual prompting strategies, some works analyze the
broader implications of prompt design choices. Deldjoo [18] con-
ducts a comparative evaluation of different hard prompting strate-
gies, such as accuracy-focused prompts, diversification prompts,
and reasoning-based formats like CoT and ICL, in the context of
provider fairness and diversity.
